background.title: People in a business
background.html:
A business has owners (for a company, its shareholders), managers who run it day to day, and staff who do the work.

  • An employee has a contract with the business: regular pay, set hours, rights such as holidays and sick pay.
  • A self-employed worker works for themselves and sells their work to the business, task by task, with no employee rights.

Unit 2 is about how a business plans, organises, leads and motivates these people. Business calls them its human resources, because people are a resource, like money or machines, that must be managed well.

background.title: Pay, costs and profit
background.html:
Money in: revenue = price × number sold. Money out: costs, such as materials, rent and pay. Profit = revenue − costs.

Staff pay is a cost. A wage is usually paid per hour or per item and often weekly; a salary is a fixed amount per year, paid monthly. A cleaner might earn a wage of $12 an hour; an accountant a salary of $48 000 a year, which is $4 000 a month.

That is why HR decisions are also money decisions: hiring, training and pay rises raise costs today, and the business hopes they raise output or quality, and so profit, later.

background.title: Who is in charge of whom
background.html:
In most organisations people report to someone: their boss gives them work and checks it. In a school, teachers report to a head of department, who reports to the principal.

Bosses have authority: the right to give instructions and make decisions. The people who report to a manager are their subordinates.

Drawing all these links as boxes and lines gives an organisation chart: the top box is the most senior person, and each row below is one level. Section 2.2 uses this picture all the time, so try drawing your own school's chart.

background.title: Why people work
background.html:
People work for money, but not only for money. Think of a part-time job: the pay matters, but so do friendly colleagues, being trusted with something important, being praised and learning new skills.

When people want to work well, managers say they are motivated. Motivated staff produce more, make fewer mistakes and stay longer, which saves the business money. When people stop caring, they are demotivated: they do the minimum, take more days off or leave.

Section 2.4 gives three theories that explain what motivates people at work, and the rewards a business can use.

background.title: How Business exam questions work
background.html:
Most questions are about a case: a short text about one business. The examiner wants business ideas used on that business.

  • The command term (explain, evaluate...) says how deep to go. Tap any command term on the page to see its meaning.
  • The marks say how much to write: "explain two reasons [4]" means two points of 2 marks each, one for the point and one for explaining it with the case.
  • Long answers (10 marks) need arguments on both sides and a judgement.

terms.def: IB command term (AO2): give a detailed account including reasons or causes. Say what happens and why, linked to the case.
IB command term (AO3): weigh up the strengths and the limitations, then reach a judgement.
IB command term (AO3): advise what the business should do, with evidence and reasons from the case.
IB command term (AO3): give a balanced review with arguments on more than one side, and a clear conclusion backed by evidence.
Assessment objective: how deep the IB goes on a topic. AO2: explain and apply to a case. AO3: evaluate, discuss or recommend. AO4: a skill, such as calculating or drawing a chart.
The instruction word in an exam question, such as explain or evaluate. It tells you what kind of answer the examiner wants.
Levels (1 to 2, 3 to 4 ... 9 to 10) used to mark a long answer. Each has a description, and your answer gets the band it fits best.
Your final decision in an evaluation, with the main reason and what it depends on: 'Yes, because..., but only if...'.
A weakness or missing piece in an argument or in the data, so you cannot be fully sure. In a 10-mark answer: what the case does not tell you.
The targets a business sets itself, such as growing sales by 10% or opening five new stores.
All the people who work for a business.
A change in a country's population: its size, ages, birth rate or education. For example, an ageing population means more people near retirement and fewer young workers.
How easily workers can change job (occupational mobility) or move to another place for work (geographical mobility).
People moving into a country to live and work. It can give businesses more workers and skills that are in short supply.
A system where staff choose when to start and finish work, as long as they work their agreed total hours.
Work made of short, one-off jobs ('gigs') paid per task, such as food deliveries, usually done by self-employed people, not employees.
Working for yourself and selling your work, not being an employee: no fixed wage, no holiday pay, but freedom to choose jobs.
Ending someone's job because of something they did, such as poor work or breaking rules. In everyday words: being sacked.
Losing your job because the job itself is no longer needed, for example after a machine takes it over. It is not the worker's fault, and the firm often pays redundancy pay.
People's health, safety and wellbeing. Staff welfare is how well the business looks after its staff.
How positive and confident staff feel about their work. Low morale means unhappy staff who work less well.
Forcing people to do something with threats, for example 'accept the change or lose your job'.
Winning over a critic by giving them a role in the change, so they stop opposing it.
Morally wrong or unfair, even if it is legal.
The right to give instructions and make decisions, which comes with a job.
A manager handing a task or decision to someone below them. Explained in 2.2.
The number of people who report directly to one manager.
The levels of an organisation from the most senior person at the top to the staff at the bottom.
The line of authority from the top to the bottom of an organisation: instructions pass down it, reports pass up.
Running an organisation with lots of formal rules, forms and procedures. Good for control, but slow.
Keeping decisions with a few people at the top, such as head office.
Passing decisions down to lower levels or to local branches.
Removing a level of the hierarchy, usually a layer of middle managers.
A structure where staff work in project teams across departments, so each person has two bosses: a department manager and a project manager.
To supervise is to watch over and check other people's work. A supervisor is a manager at the lowest level, in charge of a small team.
The most senior manager, who runs the whole company day to day. Also called the chief executive (CEO).
A large part of a company that runs one product or one region almost like a separate business.
A period when a country's economy shrinks: people spend less, firms sell less and more people lose their jobs.
A leadership style where the leader makes all decisions alone and gives orders. Explained in 2.3.
Like a parent: the leader decides alone, but in what they believe is the staff's best interest, and cares about their welfare.
A leadership style where staff are asked for their views or vote on decisions.
French for 'let them do'. The leader sets the goal and leaves staff to decide how to reach it. Say it 'less-ay fair'.
Leadership that changes style to fit the situation: the task, the staff and the time available.
Herzberg's theory, explained in 2.4: some things (hygiene factors, such as pay) only stop staff being unhappy; others (motivators, such as responsibility) make them want to work well.
Pay for each item produced, for example $0.40 per shirt. A time rate is pay per hour worked.
A fixed amount of pay per year, usually paid monthly, whatever the hours worked.
Pay that is a percentage of the value of what you sell. 5% commission on $40 000 of sales is $2 000.
Extra pay or a bonus for meeting your own targets, for example a set number of sales or excellent customer ratings.
Extra pay for staff that depends on the firm's profit: more profit, more pay.
A plan that gives staff shares in the company, free or cheaply, so they own a small part of it and gain when it does well.
Equal parts of a company's ownership. Hold 10 of its 100 shares and you own 10%. The share price is what one share costs to buy.
Benefits on top of pay, also called perks: a company car, health insurance, staff discounts, free meals.
Making a job more challenging by adding responsibility and harder tasks. Explained in 2.4.
Moving staff between different jobs or tasks from time to time, for variety.
Adding more tasks of the same difficulty to a job, for variety.
Giving staff the authority to make decisions about their own work.
Training for new staff when they start: the people, the place, the rules and the job.
Maslow's top need: becoming the best you can be, using all your talents.
Respect: from others (praise, status) and for yourself (self-respect).
To do with the body's basic needs: food, water, warmth, rest.
Money left after all costs are paid: profit = revenue − costs.
All the money from sales: price × quantity sold.
The everyday costs of running a business, such as wages, rent, energy and transport.
A prediction of a future figure, such as next year's sales or profit. It is an estimate, not a fact.
Anyone who affects or is affected by what a business does: staff, owners, customers, suppliers, the local community.
The lowest pay per hour that the law allows an employer to pay.
Teaching workers new skills so they can do a different job.
Asking people for their views before making a decision, and listening to them.
The big number that is announced first, before you look at the details.
Higher Level only. You take Business at Standard Level (SL), so HL-only content is not in your exam.
Questions asked to make the audience think, not to get an answer: 'Avez-vous remarqué que... ?'
The kind of text you write, such as a blog, a speech or a letter. Each has its own layout and tone, and IB French marks whether you chose and used the right one.
